get on nodes/proxy
get on pods/log
explain: nodes/proxy reaches the kubelet API, including exec. The good-practices page says it bypasses audit logging and admission control, and that even the get verb is enough because websocket requests are authorized as get.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Secrets: base64 is not encryption
question: An EncryptionConfiguration lists providers in the order identity, aesgcm. New Secrets are written. Are they encrypted in etcd?
options: Yes, with aesgcm
No: the first provider encrypts new writes, and identity means plain text
Only Secrets created by admins
Yes, with both providers
explain: The guide says if identity is the first provider, at-rest encryption is not enabled. The second provider is only tried when reading data it previously wrote.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a hardening map and where to practise
question: A team can do one thing this week on a cluster with no network policies, Baseline pod security, and ingress-nginx admission webhooks. Which change shrinks the most attack paths from a single compromised pod?
options: Enable debug logging
Rename the default service account
Switch base images to distroless
Default-deny network policies with explicit allows, including restricting the webhook to the API server
explain: Under default allow, any pod can reach every service, admin webhook and node port. Default deny turns one foothold into a contained one and directly blocks the IngressNightmare path. Distroless helps too, but only for the images you rebuild.

courseTitle: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
lessonTitle: Kubernetes: pods, requests versus limits, and placement
question: Nodes have 3800m allocatable CPU and 14592Mi allocatable memory. Free right now: node-a 1500m and 7592Mi, node-b 800m and 11992Mi, node-c 2000m and 2092Mi. A pod requests 1000m and 6144Mi. Which nodes are feasible?
options: node-a and node-c, because both have enough CPU
All three, because no limits were set
node-b and node-c, because each has the most of one resource
node-a only
explain: Filtering needs every requested resource to fit at the same time. node-b fails on CPU (800 < 1000) and node-c fails on memory (2092 < 6144), so only node-a clears both and scoring has one candidate. Having plenty of one resource does not help when the other is short, which is how a cluster ends up with idle CPU and nowhere to put a pod.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: The filters object and its four update operations
question: The user says *any seniority is fine*. Which state change is most faithful to what they said?
options: Leave level as it was (carryover)
Set level to null
Set level to dontcare
Reset the whole state
explain: Null and dontcare both remove the filter, but dontcare also records that the user answered the question. A system that later asks *which level?* would be asking something already answered. Carryover keeps the old filter, which is the wrong behavior here.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Plausible is not faithful: the biasing-feature test
question: Turpin et al. measure unfaithfulness only on examples where the biasing feature points to a wrong answer, using the accuracy drop. Why does that subset make accuracy a usable metric?
options: Because on that subset any answer that follows the bias is wrong, so bias-driven flips show up as lost accuracy
Because models never follow biases toward correct answers, so those examples carry no signal
Because CoT only exists on examples the model gets wrong
Because accuracy on that subset equals the fraction of CoTs that mention the bias
explain: When the bias points to a wrong option, following it costs accuracy, and the authors verified that almost all of the drop is extra bias-consistent answers rather than random noise. The bias does also push toward correct answers on the other subset (accuracy rises there). The metric says nothing directly about mentions; mentions were checked separately (1 of 426).

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: CoT monitors, and what training against them does
question: A team trains with reward = (tests pass) - penalty x (monitor flag). Flag rate falls from 30% to 2% while test pass rate rises. Which check best distinguishes real improvement from obfuscation?
options: Check that the CoTs still read fluently and stay on topic
Measure hacking with a signal independent of the CoT, such as reverting test edits or a held-out action check
Ask the trained model whether it is hacking
Re-run the same CoT monitor with a higher temperature
explain: Obfuscated CoTs are fluent and on topic by construction, and the trained policy is optimized against this monitor, so rerunning it adds little. Asking the model trusts the very channel in question. Only a behavior measure that does not route through the CoT (like Baker's revert-the-test-edits check) can reveal hacks the monitor no longer sees.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: The naive loop: four stages, one at a time
question: Someone optimizes the kernel from 24 ms to 12 ms. What is the new batch time and the new SM utilization?
options: 49 ms, utilization 24.5 percent
30.5 ms, utilization unchanged at 39.3 percent
49 ms, utilization 39.3 percent
37 ms, utilization 32.4 percent
explain: 20 + 16 + 12 + 1 = 49 ms, and the SMs are now busy 12 of those 49 ms, which is 24.5 percent. Halving the kernel bought 19.7 percent of wall time and made the imbalance worse. The 37 ms of host and copy time is where the remaining win lives.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: A worked pipeline: four chunks, and the copy-bound crossover
question: You chunk the host decode too, and measure the host stage at 8.00 ms per chunk (kernel stays 6.00 ms). What paces the pipeline and what is the 4-chunk time?
options: The host, at 8.00 ms per chunk: 18.25 + 3 x 8.00 = 42.25 ms
The kernel, at 6.00 ms per chunk: 18.25 + 3 x 6.00 = 36.25 ms
Neither; the host runs on a different device so it does not enter the makespan
The H2D copy, since it is the stage directly after the host
explain: The host is just another single-server stage in the pipeline, and the makespan is set by whichever stage is largest. At 8.00 ms it overtakes the 6.00 ms kernel, giving (8.00 + 4.00 + 6.00 + 0.25) + 3 x 8.00 = 42.25 ms, with 2.00 ms of SM idle per chunk. The fix is more host parallelism (more decode threads or loader workers), not more CUDA streams.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Packing the pair: special tokens, segments and the 512-token limit
question: A query is 20 tokens and a passage is 600 tokens. Using a BERT tokenizer with max_length 512 and truncation=True, how many passage tokens remain?
explain: Three special tokens ([CLS] and two [SEP]) plus 20 query tokens use 23 positions, leaving 512 - 23 = 489 for the passage. longest_first trims the longer side, which is the passage.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Serving it: latency for 100 candidates and distillation
question: Why does Margin-MSE train on the score difference instead of asking the student to reproduce the teacher's raw score?
options: Because the teacher's raw scores are not available after training
Because MSE cannot be computed on raw scores
Because the margin is always positive
Because different architectures produce scores on very different ranges, and ranking only depends on order and gaps
explain: The paper observed that cross-encoders, dot-product models and others have distinct score ranges. Matching margins lets the student keep its natural range while learning the teacher's preferences. The margin can even be negative when the teacher disagrees with the label.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: The one-time pad: perfect secrecy and the cost of reusing a key
question: Two ciphertexts were made with the same one-time pad. What can Eve compute without knowing the key?
options: Nothing: each ciphertext is perfectly secret
The key itself, directly
Only the lengths of the messages
The XOR of the two plaintexts
explain: XORing the ciphertexts cancels the key and leaves m1 XOR m2. From there, guessing likely words in one message reveals the other. The key itself only falls out once Eve also knows a plaintext.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Hash functions: fingerprints, avalanche and the birthday bound
question: Which property must a hash have so that nobody can create two different contracts with the same digest, one innocent and one malicious?
options: Preimage resistance
Second-preimage resistance
Avalanche effect
Collision resistance
explain: The attacker controls both documents, so they only need any pair that collides: that is collision resistance, the property MD5 and SHA-1 lost (next lesson).

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Randomness: where keys come from, and the Debian disaster
question: Why did Debian's broken generator still produce different keys on different runs, hiding the bug for almost two years?
options: The kernel added entropy later anyway
OpenSSL used the time of day
SSH re-randomised the keys
The process ID was still mixed in, giving about 32,767 variants
explain: Russ Cox notes the PID kept the output from being completely deterministic. If every key had been identical, the bug would likely have been caught quickly.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Putting it together: TLS 1.3 and the rules of using crypto
question: In TLS 1.3, which message stops a man in the middle from substituting their own Diffie-Hellman key share?
options: ClientHello
The AEAD tag on application data
The server's random value
CertificateVerify, the server's signature over the handshake
explain: The key shares are just DH values. CertificateVerify signs the transcript, including them, with the key the CA vouched for, so substituted shares fail verification.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Bleichenbacher and ROBOT: retiring RSA key exchange
question: ROBOT's authors could make facebook.com's key sign a message. Why did they say the certificate did not need to be revoked?
options: Because Facebook's certificate had already expired
Because the attack used the server as an oracle to perform operations, without extracting the private key
Because signatures made with a Bleichenbacher oracle are invalid
Because RSA keys cannot be revoked
explain: A Bleichenbacher oracle makes the server's key decrypt or sign attacker-chosen values one step at a time, but the key never leaves the server. Fixing the server (or removing RSA key exchange) closes the oracle; the key stays secret.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Secret-dependent timing: comparisons, Minerva and TPM-Fail
question: A team replaces `==` with this check: `return sum(x != y for x, y in zip(a, b)) == 0`. It visits every byte. Is it a good fix for comparing HMAC tags?
options: Yes, it is exactly as good as hmac.compare_digest
No: summing is slower than ==
No: zip silently stops at the shorter input, and hand-written loops are not guaranteed constant time; use hmac.compare_digest
Yes, as long as tags are hex strings
explain: zip stops at the shorter argument, so a short or empty tag can compare equal to a prefix (an empty tag passes). Interpreter and compiler details can also reintroduce timing differences. The standard library function is designed for this job.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Downgrade and protocol confusion: one key, one purpose
question: A team signs both webhook payloads and password-reset links with one Ed25519 key and no labels. What is the risk?
options: A signature produced for one message type may be accepted where the other is expected, if an attacker can get suitable bytes signed
Ed25519 cannot sign URLs
The key will wear out twice as fast
None, signatures are always bound to their purpose
explain: Signatures bind to bytes, not to meaning. Separate keys, or a purpose label inside the signed data, ensure a webhook signature can never be presented as a reset link signature.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Layout algebra: composition, tiling and partitioning
question: You compose a data tensor A with B and get R = A o B. Which property does the CuTe documentation guarantee?
options: R has the same shape as A
R is always injective
R(i) = A(B(i)) for all i in B's domain, and R accepts B's coordinates
R has the same strides as B
explain: Composition's post-conditions are compatible(B, R) and R(i) == A(B(i)). B defines the domain, so R takes B's coordinates; A defines where those land.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Why servers strand DRAM and why DDR alone cannot fix it
question: Why can't a CPU vendor simply add many more DDR5 channels to every socket?
options: DDR5 does not support more than two channels per socket
More channels would make memory non-coherent
Each DDR5 channel is a wide parallel interface that needs many pins (Sun et al. cite 288 per channel), and the package pin budget is fixed
Linux cannot address more than eight memory channels
explain: DDR is a wide parallel interface. Capacity and bandwidth scale with the number of channels, and each channel eats a lot of pins. A serial CXL link delivers more bandwidth per pin, which is why it is attractive for expansion.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Placing pages: tiering in Linux, pooling in Pond
question: TPP does not promote a slow-tier page on its first NUMA hinting fault if the page is on the inactive LRU list. What problem does this avoid?
options: Deadlock between the fault handler and reclaim
Ping-pong: an infrequently used page is promoted, then quickly demoted again, wasting migration bandwidth
Running out of tier-16 memory
Breaking cache coherence on the CXL link
explain: A single touch does not prove a page is hot. Promoting it would push something else out of DRAM, and under pressure the promoted page would soon be demoted again. Requiring the page to be on the active LRU adds hysteresis: a page must show repeated use before it moves, so it stops flipping back and forth.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: View source is not hacking: the Missouri teachers' SSNs (2021)
question: Which statement about Base64 is correct?
options: It is a weak form of encryption that needs a short key
It is an encoding that anyone can reverse without a key, so it protects nothing
It is a hash, so the original cannot be recovered
It is only used for images
explain: Base64 (RFC 4648) maps bytes to 64 printable characters so they survive text channels. Decoding needs no secret. When officials said the reporter had 'unencrypted the source code' or 'decoded the HTML source code', they made an ordinary step sound like an attack.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Copyright and trade secrets: DMCA section 1201 and Megamos Crypto
question: Which change did the 2021 rulemaking make to the security research exemption, according to GitHub's summary?
options: It made circumvention tools legal to sell
It removed the condition that the research must not violate any other law
It ended the exemption
It extended the exemption to servers you do not own without permission
explain: GitHub explains that before 2021 a violation of another law such as the CFAA could also cost you the DMCA exemption. The Office recommended removing that condition, while noting researchers must still consider other laws themselves.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Professional ethics: ISC2, ACM, the Menlo Report and the UMN patches
question: Under the ISC2 complaint procedure, who may complain that a member breached Canon III (diligent and competent service to principals)?
options: Any member of the public
Only principals, meaning those with an employer or contractor relationship with the member
Only other certified professionals
Nobody: Canon III is advisory
explain: ISC2's procedure says anyone may complain about Canons I or II, only principals about Canon III, and only other professionals who subscribe to a code of ethics about Canon IV.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Why the pretraining mixture is a decision you cannot skip
question: Why is tuning the mixture directly on downstream benchmarks risky, beyond its cost?
options: Benchmarks are measured in accuracy, not loss
Downstream tuning always picks uniform weights
The mixture can overfit to the specific benchmarks used, which may not reflect the many tasks the model will face
explain: A pretrained model is used for many tasks nobody listed in advance. A mixture tuned to a handful of benchmarks can trade away performance elsewhere. DoReMi deliberately uses no downstream data.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Knobs, failure modes, and what came after DoReMi
question: You start DoReMi from uniform reference weights on a corpus where one domain is tiny. After one round, results are no better than baseline. What is the paper's recommended next move?
options: Run iterated DoReMi: train a new reference model on the round-1 weights and run again
Increase the proxy to 1B parameters
Set the smoothing c to 0 so weak domains disappear
Copy the published Pile weights
explain: On GLaM, round 1 from uniform weights was only comparable to the baseline, and round 2 matched downstream-tuned weights. A suboptimal reference gives a suboptimal excess loss; iterating fixes the reference. Bigger proxies did worse in the paper.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Cleaning the crawl: heuristic rules, perplexity filters, exact dedup
question: Why do pipelines run heuristic rules before a perplexity filter or a model-based classifier?
options: Rules are more accurate than models
The order does not matter for cost
Rules only count words and symbols, so they cheaply remove obvious junk before the expensive model-based steps run
Perplexity filters only work on text that has been deduplicated
explain: A rule is a few counts per page; a language model or classifier must process every token. Removing describable junk first shrinks what the costly steps must score. Orders still vary between pipelines.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: SIMD lanes: contiguous loads, gathers, and blocked SoA
question: In `soa<8> Point pts[...]` (float x, y, z), what is the byte offset of `pts[17].z` from the start of the array?
explain: Block 2 (17 divided by 8 is 2, rounded down), lane 1 (the remainder). Each block is 96 bytes and z is the third 32-byte run. Offset = 2 x 96 + 2 x 32 + 1 x 4 = 260. 212 is the AoS answer (17 x 12 + 8), 204 is where record 17 starts in AoS, and 68 is plain SoA (17 x 4).

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Finding sensitive data: inventories, patterns, checksums and context
question: A Purview-style rule finds a Luhn-valid 16-digit number with no keywords or dates within 300 characters. What should the confidence be?
options: Low: pattern and checksum without supporting context
High: the checksum proves it is a card
None: without a keyword it is discarded
High, because test numbers are excluded
explain: In Microsoft's documented definition, pattern plus checksum alone is the low-confidence pattern (65). High confidence (85) needs one of the context conditions. About 1 in 10 random numbers pass Luhn, so the checksum alone proves little.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Searching encrypted data: deterministic encryption and enclaves
question: A team wants to encrypt an `is_vip` boolean column but still filter on it. Why is deterministic encryption a poor choice?
options: Deterministic encryption cannot encrypt booleans
It is slower than randomized encryption
It requires a secure enclave
With only two values, each ciphertext appears in many rows, and counting them (plus any known fact about one row) reveals every row's value
explain: Deterministic encryption maps each plaintext to one ciphertext. With two possible values, there are two ciphertexts; knowing the VIP rate or one VIP customer decodes all rows. Microsoft's documentation warns about exactly this for True/False columns.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: How DLP recognises sensitive content
question: A DLP rule has 95% recall and a 1% false positive rate. Real leaks are 1 in 1,000 messages. Roughly what share of its alerts are real?
options: About 9%
About 95%
About 50%
About 1%
explain: Per 200,000 messages: 190 true alerts and about 1,998 false ones, so 190 / 2,188 is about 8.7%. Recall is 95%, but precision is low because clean messages vastly outnumber leaks.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Disposal as a process: Morgan Stanley's drives and the certificate
question: Branch servers had disk encryption switched on years after deployment, and the product encrypted only newly written data. Why does a later cryptographic erase not sanitise them?
options: The data written before encryption was enabled is still plaintext on the disks, and destroying the key does nothing to it
Crypto erase never works on servers
The keys were too short
Crypto erase needs internet access
explain: Cryptographic erase only removes access to what was encrypted. SP 800-88 Rev. 2 makes 'no sensitive data previously stored in plaintext' a precondition, and the SEC order describes exactly this flaw.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: What Internet honeypots see: noise, bots and reused passwords
question: Your new Internet-facing SSH honeypot logged 20,000 login attempts overnight. What is the right conclusion?
options: You are being targeted by a skilled group and should start incident response
Bots only try SSH, so other services are safe
The honeypot is misconfigured, since nobody knows its address
This is normal background noise; analyse it for trends rather than treating it as an incident
explain: Any public address is scanned constantly by automated tools. Volume alone says nothing about targeting; patterns, new exploits and overlap with your own logs do.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Honey records and honeywords: decoys inside your data
question: You put a different honey record in each of four copies of a customer table. A trap address from the analytics copy starts receiving spam. What do you learn?
options: Nothing, honey records only show that some breach happened
That the analytics copy (or something it was exported to) leaked
That the production database is compromised
That the spam filter has failed
explain: Unique records per copy turn a late alert into a scoping clue: the leak path runs through the copy that held that record.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Measuring value: the Tularosa study, metrics and practice
question: In the Tularosa Study, what does "every participant in a Present condition triggered a decoy alert before reporting a successful exploit of a real machine" imply for defenders?
options: Decoy alerts gave warning before the real damage, which is the time a response team needs
Decoys prevented all exploitation
Participants recognised every decoy
Telling attackers about deception makes decoys useless
explain: The decoys did not stop every attack (exploit successes fell but were not zero); they consistently fired first, which is the early warning deception promises.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Seeds and RNG state: a different problem from kernels
question: Greedy decoding at temperature 0 consumes no random numbers. Does that make a server reproducible?
options: Yes. With no RNG in the path, the output is a pure function of the prompt and the weights.
Yes, as long as the seed is also pinned for the workers.
No, because temperature 0 is implemented as a very small positive temperature and still samples.
No. It removes the RNG, but the hard argmax turns an arbitrarily small logit difference into a different token.
explain: Greedy is a pure function of the logits, and the logits are not a pure function of the prompt in a batching server. Removing the RNG removes one source and makes the remaining one maximally visible, since argmax has no tolerance at a near-tie.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Making rare states common: faults, BUGGIFY and swarm testing
question: Using FoundationDB's defaults, what is the probability that two specific buggify sites are *both* activated in the same run?
explain: Each site is activated independently with probability 0.25 once per run, so both are active with $0.25 \times 0.25 = 0.0625$, about 1 run in 16. Rare pairs still happen often across tens of thousands of runs per night.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Threat-modelling a pipeline: poisoned pipeline execution
question: A team stores the pipeline definition in a separate repository that only the platform team can edit. The pipeline runs `npm test` on every developer branch with a registry token in the environment. Are they safe from PPE?
options: No: this is the indirect form. Anyone who can push a branch can change package.json scripts or test files that npm test runs
Yes, because the CI file cannot be edited by developers
Yes, as long as the token is masked in logs
No, but only if the repository is public
explain: OWASP lists exactly this as I-PPE: the CI config is protected, but files it executes are not. Masking only hides values in logs; code that runs can still send the token anywhere.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: OIDC from CI, precisely: subject claims and environments
question: A team's apply role trusts `StringLike` `repo:acme/infra:ref:refs/heads/*`. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: it pins the repository
It accepts tokens from other organisations
StringLike cannot be used with OIDC
It accepts tokens from every branch, so a pushed feature branch can assume the apply role
explain: The * matches any branch name. Trust the environment subject exactly, and let the environment's branch rule decide which branch may deploy.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Scanners in the pipeline: Checkov, Trivy and zizmor
question: Checkov passes a workflow that uses pull_request_target and checks out the PR head commit, while zizmor fails it. What is the right conclusion?
options: Checkov is broken and should be removed
The workflow is safe because one scanner passed it
Tools have different rule sets; run a workflow-specific analyser alongside a general IaC scanner, and treat a pass as "no known pattern found", not "safe"
zizmor is wrong, because pull_request_target is required for forks
explain: In the real run only zizmor's dangerous-triggers audit flagged the pwn request. A clean scan only means no rule matched.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a secure pipeline, a response plan, practice
question: In the finished pipeline, why do pull requests get a separate read-only plan role instead of the apply role?
options: PR code is untrusted and plan can run provider or PR-controlled code; a read-only role means that code cannot change the cloud even if it runs
Read-only roles are faster
The apply role cannot run terraform plan
GitHub forbids write roles on pull requests
explain: Lessons 2 and 9: anything that runs during a PR may be attacker-controlled. Giving it only read access caps the damage, while reviewers still see a real plan.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Training: a weighted average of masked-LM losses
question: Why does training on t drawn from all of [0, 1] matter for generation, compared with BERT's fixed 15%?
options: Generation starts from a fully masked sequence, so the model must be good at predicting with almost no context; a fixed 15% ratio never trains that regime
Uniform t makes training cheaper per step
It lets the model use a causal mask
It removes the need for a tokenizer
explain: Sampling walks t from 1 down to 0, visiting every masking ratio. A model that only ever saw 15% masks has never learned the early, nearly empty steps, and its loss is not a likelihood bound.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Making diffusion LMs useful: AR initialization, RL and remasking
question: A team runs DPO on a diffusion LM and estimates each of the four ELBOs (policy and reference, chosen and rejected) with its own fresh random masks. Training is unstable. What is the cheapest fix?
options: Switch to a causal attention mask during DPO
Lower the learning rate until the noise averages out
Estimate each ELBO with a single timestep and many masks at that timestep
Use the same timesteps and masks for the policy and reference estimates of each answer
explain: Antithetic sampling costs nothing extra: the policy and reference ELBOs share their randomness, so their errors cancel in the log-ratio that DPO uses. Spending a budget on one timestep with many masks is worse than spreading it over timesteps, and a smaller step size only slows learning.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Moving the KV cache: bytes, links and overlap
question: A team streams KV layer by layer, so per-request exposed transfer is only 10 ms. At peak, prefill GPUs produce 40 GB/s of KV, and the shared link carries 25 GB/s. What happens?
options: TTFT rises slightly but TPOT is unaffected
Decode GPUs simply run larger batches
Nothing, because overlap already hid the transfer
Transfers queue up without bound: the link cannot sustain the KV production rate, so decode starts slip further and prefill memory fills
explain: Overlap hides one transfer behind compute, but sustained bandwidth must still exceed rate x KV bytes. At 40 GB/s produced against 25 GB/s carried, the backlog grows. DistServe's 90 Gbps example is exactly this throughput check.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: NTFS and the master file table, record by record
question: Your parser reads an MFT record without applying fixups. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing: fixups only matter for directories
The FILE signature is missing, so the record is skipped
Two bytes at the end of each 512-byte stride are wrong, which can corrupt any attribute that crosses a stride boundary
All timestamps are shifted by 100 nanoseconds
explain: The stride ends hold the update sequence number, not the real data. Attributes spanning byte 510 to 511 or 1022 to 1023 read wrong values. Fixups apply to all records, the signature is at the start and unaffected, and timestamps are not shifted.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: APFS: containers, copy-on-write and snapshots
question: A suspect deleted a document from their Mac at 15:00. The volume has a snapshot from 14:30. What can you expect?
options: Nothing: APFS overwrites deleted files immediately
The document is in the snapshot only if it was saved after 15:00
The 14:30 snapshot still contains the document as it was at 14:30
Snapshots hold only metadata, never file content
explain: A snapshot is a read-only copy of the file system at its creation time and keeps referenced blocks alive. Later deletion from the live volume does not touch it.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: SRUM and browser history: network use and what was visited
question: A Chrome visit_time is 13416934350000000. Which conversion gives the Unix time in seconds?
explain: Chromium counts microseconds since 1601, so divide by one million and subtract the 11,644,473,600 seconds between 1601 and 1970. Dividing by ten million would be FILETIME's 100 ns ticks; skipping the subtraction gives a date in 2395.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Trusting your tools: Cellebrite, Signal (2021) and validation
question: An examiner hashes a phone extraction before and after analysis and the hashes match. Why could the report still be wrong, per Signal's 2021 findings?
options: Code running on the analysis machine could alter reports without changing the extraction's hash
Hashes of phone extractions are unreliable
Matching hashes mean the extraction was empty
The phone may have changed after extraction
explain: The hash covers the evidence input. Signal described malicious files that could alter Cellebrite reports with no detectable timestamp changes or checksum failures, i.e. the output, not the input.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: DiskANN search: beam width, SSD reads and re-ranking
question: Why does DiskANN's re-ranking with full-precision vectors cost no extra SSD reads?
options: Full vectors are cached in RAM
Each node's full vector is stored in the same disk block as its neighbor list, so it arrives with the read the search already made
Re-ranking uses PQ codes only
It reads all candidates in one big sequential read
explain: The record layout puts the vector next to the adjacency list, inside one 4 KB read. Re-ranking piggybacks on reads the beam search needed anyway. The paper contrasts this with an earlier system that fetched about a hundred candidate vectors at the end, in one burst of random reads.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: The DPO loss on one preference pair, with real numbers
question: At step 0 the policy equals the reference. What is the DPO loss of every pair, and what is each pair's gradient weight?
options: Loss 0 and weight 0, since nothing has changed
Loss 1 and weight 1
It depends on how strongly the reference prefers y_w
Loss ln 2 (about 0.693) and weight 0.5
explain: All log-ratios are 0, so the margin is 0 for every pair regardless of the reference's own preference. $-\log \sigma(0) = \ln 2 \approx 0.693$ and the weight is $\sigma(0) = 0.5$. The reference's preference cancels because DPO only scores improvement over the reference.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: KTO: aligning with thumbs up and thumbs down, no pairs
question: Why does KTO estimate $z_0$ from mismatched (prompt, other example's output) pairs instead of each example's own output?
options: Because own outputs are usually chosen to be clearly good or bad, so their rewards are unrepresentatively large
Because mismatched pairs need no forward pass
Because the own output's log-ratio is always zero
Because it makes the estimate unbiased
explain: The paper says matched outputs have often been deliberately picked as canonically good or bad, giving high-magnitude rewards that would skew the reference point. The mismatched estimate still costs an extra forward pass and is explicitly biased (clamping adds upward bias), but it is cheap and stable.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Why a live data migration needs four careful phases
question: Which step is the real point of no return, where undoing it needs more than flipping a flag back?
options: Starting dual writes
Switching reads to the new store
Switching writes to the new store while still archiving to the old one
Stopping writes to the old store and deleting its data
explain: As long as some code keeps the old store current (dual writes in phases 1 to 3, archiving in phase 3), you can point traffic back at it. Once old writes stop and its data is deleted, going back would mean a new migration in the other direction.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Flipping writes, cutting over and deleting the old path
question: A gh-ost migration's applier is 6,000 events behind and applies 10,000 events per second. Using the simplified model, roughly how long are writes blocked during cut-over?
options: About 6 ms
About 60 ms
About 600 ms
About 6 seconds
explain: 6,000 events at 10,000 events per second take 0.6 s. That is why tools throttle and wait for lag to be small before cutting over: the write pause grows with the backlog.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Maps: counting, histograms and timing in the kernel
question: You remove the /has_key(@start, tid)/ filter from the timing script. What do you most likely see?
options: Nothing changes
The verifier rejects the script
A few enormous durations near the system uptime, from calls that started before tracing began and read a start time of 0
Every duration becomes 0
explain: Calls already in flight at attach time only hit the return probe. Their @start[tid] reads as 0, so nsecs - 0 equals the time since boot, which pollutes the top buckets of the histogram.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Affine quantization: storing reals as int8 plus a scale
question: Why does the quantization scheme require that real 0 maps exactly to an integer code?
options: Because int8 cannot store negative numbers
Because zero padding and ReLU zeros would otherwise all carry the same rounding error, acting as a systematic bias
Because the scale S must be an integer
Because dequantization divides by zero otherwise
explain: Zero padding inserts many zeros at borders and ReLU creates many exact zeros. If 0 were not on the grid, they would all round to the same nonzero value, a biased error repeated across the tensor. Jacob et al. and the ONNX Runtime docs both call this requirement out.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Edge devices: the doors attackers now try first
question: Why is a VPN gateway often a more valuable target than an employee laptop?
options: It usually has a faster processor
Laptops cannot be attacked over the network
VPN traffic is not encrypted
Anyone can reach it before login, it holds credentials with reach inside, and it usually runs no EDR
explain: The three properties together: pre-authentication exposure, a privileged position (passwords, service accounts, routes inside) and little monitoring. A laptop typically has EDR and must first be reached through phishing.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Ivanti Connect Secure, 2024: chained zero-days and a fooled checker
question: Why did the toy on-box integrity checker report nothing on a backdoored appliance?
options: Its known-good hashes were wrong
SHA-256 is broken
It only checks files in /tmp
The intruder had root and edited the skip list the checker reads from the same device
explain: The manifest was correct. The checker trusted configuration stored on the device it was checking. Volexity found the real attacker adding entries to the ICT's files; CISA later found even the external ICT missed compromises.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Management interfaces: keep the admin door off the internet
question: Which setup meets BOD 23-02 for a firewall's web admin page?
options: The admin page stays on the internet with a long password
The admin page is moved to port 18443 so scanners miss it
The admin page is public but logs every login
The admin page answers only on an isolated management network reached from admin workstations
explain: BOD 23-02 accepts two options: remove the interface from the internet, or put a separate policy enforcement point in front of it. A strong password, an unusual port or logging leave the interface itself reachable.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Overthinking: 901 tokens to say 2 + 3 = 5
question: A reasoning model's response has 5 solutions; the first correct answer appears in solution 1 (60 tokens) and the response is 600 tokens. A colleague says 'truncate every response after solution 1 and nothing is lost'. What does Chen et al.'s data say?
options: Correct: later solutions never change the answer, so truncation is free
Mostly right for easy sets, but on hard sets later rounds sometimes fix a wrong first answer, and the authors keep one reflection round for that reason
Wrong: later solutions are where most correct answers first appear
Wrong: the first solution is usually the longest, so truncating saves little
explain: Over 92% of correct responses are already correct at solution 1, which is why the waste is large. But not 100%: keeping only the first correct solution (FCS) lowered MATH500 accuracy, so their best recipe keeps one extra reflection round (lesson 2).

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Length penalties inside RL: Kimi k1.5 and DAPO
question: You train with the Arora-Zanette reward and GRPO's std-normalized advantages. On prompts where all 8 samples are correct, you double alpha from 0.1 to 0.2. What happens to the advantages in those groups?
options: They double, so the push toward short answers doubles
Nothing: alpha cancels between the deviation and the std, so the advantages are identical
They halve, because the std grows faster than the deviation
They become zero, because all samples are correct
explain: Every reward is $1 - \alpha f_i$, so both the deviation from the mean and the std scale with alpha and the ratio does not. Zero would be right for a correctness-only reward; here the length term breaks the tie. To keep alpha meaningful, use the plain deviation (no std), as Arora and Zanette do.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: One input, many readers: where encoding bugs come from
question: Which situation is a parser differential?
options: A proxy and the server behind it decide differently where an HTTP request ends
A function crashes on an empty string
One library is slower than another at parsing JSON
A parser rejects input that breaks the specification
explain: A differential is two parsers reaching different results from the same input. Speed, crashes on edge cases and strict rejection are not disagreements between two readers.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Unicode normalisation: NFC, NFD, NFKC and NFKD
question: A file name check rejects `/` and `..`, then the code stores `normalize("NFKC", name)`. What is wrong?
options: NFKC can produce `/` and `.` from fullwidth characters after the check has run
Nothing; NFKC only changes accents
NFKC is slower than NFC
NFKC turns file names upper-case
explain: Fullwidth full stop and fullwidth solidus normalise to `.` and `/`. Normalise first, then check the normalised value, then use that same value.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Confusables and homoglyphs: UTS #39 skeletons
question: Why should you not display or store the skeleton as the user's name?
options: Skeletons are a comparison key that can change the visible text, for example m becomes rn
Skeletons are encrypted
Skeletons are always upper-case
Skeletons remove all digits
explain: A skeleton maps characters to look-alike prototypes, which may be different characters or even sequences (`m` to `rn`). Keep the canonical name for identity and use the skeleton only to detect collisions.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: JSON differentials: duplicate keys, numbers and CouchDB
question: A Go service decodes a quantity as a float64 and a Python service as an int. For which quantity can they first disagree?
explain: Doubles represent every integer up to 2^53 = 9007199254740992 exactly. 9007199254740993 is the first integer that rounds (to ...992). The other values are exact in both.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: From antivirus to EDR: sensor, cloud, console and response
question: Ana's laptop runs signature antivirus only. Word starts PowerShell, which downloads nothing to disk and connects to a remote server. Why might the antivirus stay silent?
options: It judges files one at a time, and no file here matches a known-bad signature; the suspicious part is the sequence of behaviours
Antivirus cannot run on laptops that have Office installed
PowerShell disables antivirus whenever it starts
Antivirus only scans email, never processes
explain: Signature antivirus answers a per-file question. Each file here (winword.exe, powershell.exe) is legitimate. The signal is in the relationships: an Office app starting a shell that then goes online. Recording and correlating those relationships is what EDR adds.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Sysmon configuration: include, exclude and rule groups
question: An admin writes `<ProcessAccess onmatch="include" />` with no rules inside, expecting to see every process access. What does Sysmon log for event 10?
options: Every process access
Only access to lsass.exe
Nothing
Only accesses by unsigned programs
explain: An include filter logs only events that match a rule; with no rules nothing matches, so nothing is logged. To log everything you would use an empty exclude filter (which is usually far too noisy for event 10).

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Application control I: allowlisting and AppLocker
question: A path rule allows `C:\Windows\*`. Why is that weaker than a publisher rule for Microsoft-signed binaries?
options: Path rules are slower to evaluate
Publisher rules also block Microsoft Office
Some folders under `C:\Windows` are writable by ordinary users, so anything a user copies there is allowed; a publisher rule requires the file's signature instead
Path rules only work for DLLs
explain: A path rule trusts a location. Microsoft's default-rules page names `C:\Windows\Temp` as user-writable, so a path rule over the Windows folder lets users run their own files from there. A publisher rule trusts a signature the user cannot forge.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: What EDR can and cannot see
question: Which of these would an endpoint sensor on employees' laptops record?
options: A forwarding rule created in cloud webmail from the attacker's own browser
A login to the company VPN appliance
powershell.exe on a laptop opening a handle to lsass.exe
The content of a TLS connection to a web server
explain: Process-to-process handle requests on a monitored host are exactly what sensors record. The webmail rule and VPN login happen on systems with no sensor, and TLS content is encrypted; only metadata such as the destination is visible.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Hart's NALM: steady states, step changes and signatures
question: A 1500 W kettle and a 1500 W space heater (both nearly resistive) live in the same house. Which feature from Hart's pipeline separates them best?
options: Nothing in a single (dP, dQ) step; you need other cues such as typical duration or time of day
Their reactive power steps, since dQ differs
Voltage normalisation, since it rescales each appliance differently
The steady-state tolerance of 35 W
explain: Both are resistive, so dQ is near zero for both and dP matches: the two points land in one cluster. Reactive power only helps when the loads differ in it. Normalisation is applied to the aggregate, not per appliance. Separating them needs extra features such as on-duration or usage patterns, which is why later models add temporal structure.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Why raw strings break filters and joins
question: A team stores only the canonical company ID and discards the raw string to save space. What goes wrong first?
options: Nothing: the canonical ID carries all the information that was in the raw string
Filters become slower because IDs are longer than names
When the matcher makes a mistake or the taxonomy changes, there is no way to audit or re-run normalization on the original input
Fuzzy matching stops working because IDs cannot be compared with edit distance
explain: Normalization is a lossy, model-driven step that will be wrong sometimes and will be improved over time. Keeping the raw string lets you show members what they typed, debug bad merges and re-normalize everything when the alias table or model changes.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: From pairwise links to entities: clustering
question: Your entity graph has a cluster of 40,000 company records that should be about 30 companies. What is the most likely cause?
options: Blocking was too strict
A few false links between large clusters, chained by transitive connected components
The prior lambda was set too low
explain: Strict blocking and a low prior both cause missed links, which make clusters too small. Giant clusters come from false edges: connected components chains them, so one bad edge between two big clusters merges both.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: App registrations vs service principals: how an app gets an identity
question: Which audit activity best catches someone quietly taking over an existing powerful app in your tenant?
options: Update application - Certificates and secrets management (or Add service principal credentials)
Add user
Consent to application
Register device
explain: Taking over an existing app means adding a credential to it, which logs as a certificates and secrets update on the application or added service principal credentials. Consent and new users are other steps of other patterns.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Device code phishing: Storm-2372 and signing in for someone else
question: A tenant blocks device code flow everywhere except for the SharePoint resource. A user's session began with a device code sign-in to SharePoint. They then try to open Exchange Online in the same session. What does Microsoft document?
options: Exchange is blocked, because the session is protocol tracked and the device code policy applies to later requests from it
Exchange is allowed because the user signed in normally
Exchange prompts for a new device code
The policy is ignored for refresh tokens
explain: Microsoft's example is exactly this: protocol tracking keeps the session marked as device code through later refreshes, so a sign-in to Exchange in that session is blocked by the authentication flows policy.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Hybrid identity: Entra Connect, PTA, Seamless SSO and Tier 0
question: Why does Microsoft recommend rolling the AZUREADSSOACC Kerberos decryption key at least every 30 days?
options: Because anyone holding a copy of that key can create tickets Entra ID trusts for synced users, so a regular rollover limits how long a stolen copy stays useful
Because Kerberos tickets expire after 30 days
To change the encryption from AES to RC4
Because the key is needed to sync passwords
explain: Entra ID decrypts Seamless SSO tickets with that key, so a stolen copy works like a silver ticket key for the cloud sign-in. Rolling it regularly, and after any AD compromise, retires old copies.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Why one thread per connection stops scaling
question: Why do event loops set O_NONBLOCK on every socket even though they only read sockets the kernel reported as ready?
options: Because epoll refuses to watch blocking sockets
Because nonblocking reads are faster to copy
Because readiness can be spurious, and one blocking read would stall every other client on the loop
Because blocking sockets cannot be written to
explain: epoll watches blocking sockets just fine. But a readiness report is only a hint: the data may have been discarded, or another thread may have consumed it. With a blocking socket that read would put the only loop thread to sleep, and every other connection would wait with it.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Event loops in practice: libuv, timers, thread pools
question: The only active timer is due in 250 ms, no idle handles are active and nothing is closing. What timeout does libuv pass to the poll step?
options: 0, so it can check the timer often
-1 (infinite), since timers are handled separately
250 ms: sleep until the nearest timer is due unless I/O arrives first
10 ms, a fixed tick
explain: The libuv rules give 0 only when the loop is stopping, has nothing active, has idle handles, or is closing handles. Otherwise the timeout is the time until the closest timer, and infinity only when there are no timers. The I/O wait and the timer wait are one blocking call.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Testing many variants: Bonferroni and Holm corrections
question: Why did the 17 null variants in the concrete run look better than the baseline on average?
options: The paired t-test is biased toward the variant
Every comparison reused the same baseline run, which happened to score low on these queries, so the tests are correlated
Holm correction shifts p-values downward
The variants were trained on the test queries
explain: The baseline scored 0.357 while its true quality is 0.402. Every variant was compared to that one unlucky draw, so they all looked better together. Shared baselines make multiple tests correlated, which is why the observed FWER (0.421) differs from the independence formula (0.642).

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Why attackers then reuse existing code
question: Why did NX alone not end memory-corruption exploits?
options: Because NX can be turned off by any program
Because NX only applies to 32-bit processes
Because NX leaks the canary
Because attackers could still redirect control to code that is already executable, such as functions and instruction sequences in libc
explain: NX blocks running data as code, but a hijacked return or function pointer can target existing executable code. That is the core insight of return-into-libc and of Shacham's return-oriented programming paper.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Protecting returns: shadow stacks and pointer authentication
question: An overflow writes past a buffer using an index, skipping the canary and changing only the saved return address. Which mitigation still catches it at return?
options: A hardware shadow stack, because it compares the return address itself with a protected copy
The stack canary
FORTIFY_SOURCE
Partial RELRO
explain: The canary is untouched, so its check passes. The shadow stack compares the actual return address with a copy that normal stores cannot change, so any modification is caught.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Turning mitigations on and checking a binary
question: `readelf -lW prog` shows a GNU_RELRO segment, and `readelf -d prog` shows `FLAGS_1 PIE` but no BIND_NOW or NOW flag. What should you conclude?
options: Partial RELRO and PIE: .got.plt is still writable; add -Wl,-z,now
Full RELRO and PIE
No RELRO, because BIND_NOW is missing
Not PIE, because BIND_NOW is missing
explain: GNU_RELRO alone is partial RELRO. Full RELRO also needs immediate binding (BIND_NOW / NOW). PIE is indicated separately by the PIE flag and the DYN file type.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Putting a price on the ping-pong
question: Under the model with h = 1, C = 100 and b = 50, what is the slowdown S for 8 threads sharing one line?
explain: S = k(1 + C/(b h)) = 8 x (1 + 100/50) = 8 x 3 = 24. The 808 answer is the b = 1 worst case, and 3 forgets to multiply by k: all k threads' writes go through one line, one at a time.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: FedAvg exactly, worked on three clients over two rounds
question: Client A (54 examples) returns 0.10, client B (36) returns 0.80, client C (18) returns 2.70, but this round client B drops out and never reports. What does FedAvg set as the new global model?
options: 0.767, since the weights 54/108, 36/108 and 18/108 are properties of the clients
0.500, the weighted average with client B's contribution set to zero
0.750, the weighted average of A and C renormalized over 72 examples
The round is discarded, because FedAvg requires every selected client
explain: The denominator is m_t, the examples in this round only: 54 + 18 = 72. So the model is (54/72) x 0.10 + (18/72) x 2.70 = 0.075 + 0.675 = 0.750. Keeping stale weights that sum to less than one (option B) would shrink the model toward zero, and single dropouts never abandon a round.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Non-IID data and client drift: fast convergence to the wrong answer
question: Why is SCAFFOLD usually described as a better fit for cross-silo than for cross-device federated learning?
options: It requires every client to keep its control variate across rounds and doubles the upload, while phones are stateless and rarely selected twice
It needs a GPU on every client
Its server update is incompatible with weighted averaging
It only converges when every client holds IID data
explain: The variate c_i is per-client state carried from one participation to the next, and the upload carries a model delta plus a variate delta. Ten hospitals that join every round can do both; a phone that participates once in a training run never gets to use its variate.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: What the server sees: secure aggregation and differential privacy
question: Why did Gboard's production training move from DP-FedAvg's accounting to DP-FTRL?
options: DP-FTRL needs no clipping
DP-FTRL does not add noise, so accuracy is higher
Secure aggregation cannot be used with DP-FedAvg
DP-FedAvg's best guarantees rely on amplification by sampling, which needs uniformly random client selection that a device fleet cannot guarantee
explain: Devices are eligible only when idle, charging and on an unmetered network, so the server cannot sample users uniformly, and the sampling-based accountant's assumption breaks. DP-FTRL adds tree-correlated noise to prefix sums of updates and gets its guarantee from bounding how often and how close together a client participates.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: ACORN-1: expand at search time instead of build time
question: In the codetrace, why is J returned even though J is not in H's stored list?
options: J is H's entry point on the level
J was recovered from H's compressed M_beta entries
Truncation to M adds the next closest node
The lookup reads failing neighbor G's list and J passes the predicate
explain: ACORN-1 expands every neighbor u of H, including ones that fail, into u's own list, then filters. G fails but links to J, so J appears. There is no M_beta compression in ACORN-1 (it is fixed at M_beta = M).

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Shared experts: an always-on path for common knowledge
question: Two teams report opposite results on shared experts: DeepSeekMoE finds them essential, OLMoE finds a shared expert slightly worse than an extra routed one. Which statement is best supported?
options: One of the two experiments must be wrong
Shared experts only help with softmax routers
It is open: the answer depends on granularity, combinations given up and balancing, and the 2.414 result measures a trained model's dependence, not a from-scratch comparison
Shared experts always help but cost more FLOPs
explain: Both are careful experiments with different designs. OLMoE compared two models trained from scratch at equal compute; DeepSeekMoE's from-scratch ablation was on a coarse GShard-style model, and its 2.414 number comes from disabling the expert after training. Later designs went both ways (V3 kept one; Qwen3 dropped them).

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Below the operating system: why boot code is the deepest foothold
question: An incident responder wipes a server's disks and reinstalls the OS, but the same backdoor reappears within minutes of the first boot. Which location best explains this?
options: A scheduled task in the new OS image
A browser extension synced from the cloud
An implant in the motherboard's SPI flash that rewrites the backdoor at boot
A malicious kernel module on the old disk
explain: Only the SPI flash survives a disk wipe and reinstall. A firmware implant such as LoJax (lesson 15) drops its payload into the fresh OS on every boot. The old disk is gone, and a fresh image has no scheduled task unless something wrote one.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: How firmware decides to run an image: db, dbx and the chain
question: db trusts the CA 'Contoso Boot CA'. dbx contains the certificate of one leaf that CA issued. An image is signed by a *different* leaf from the same CA. What happens?
options: Allowed: the CA is in db and nothing in this image's chain is in dbx
Rejected, because the CA is linked to a revoked leaf
Rejected, because dbx entries apply to all images
Allowed only if its hash is in db
explain: dbx is checked against the hash and the certificates in this image's own chain. The revoked leaf is not in it, and the CA in db verifies it, so it runs.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Measured boot: PCRs, extend and what each PCR records
question: Malware running in the kernel wants PCR4 to hold the clean value fbebf1... again. Why can it not do that?
options: PCR4 is encrypted
The kernel cannot talk to the TPM
PCR4 is reset by every dbx update
It can only extend, and no sequence of further extends returns to an earlier value without a TPM reset, which means a reboot
explain: Extend is one-way: the new value hashes the old one. Reaching a target value would require finding a hash preimage. Only a platform reset clears PCRs 0 to 15, and then the boot is measured again from scratch.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Case: LogoFAIL, a boot logo parsed by the most trusted code
question: A vendor fixes the overflow by checking `if (width * 2 < width) reject;` in uint32 arithmetic, and also multiplies by height later without a check. Is the fix complete?
options: Yes, the doubling was the only overflow
Yes, because height is always small
No, because the check itself always rejects
No: row times height can still wrap; every multiplication feeding a size needs a range or overflow check
explain: The toy shows two multiplications. Checking one leaves the other. Bounding width and height first, then computing in a wider type, closes both.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: Online softmax: exact attention one block at a time
question: Besides the output tile $O_i$, what does the FlashAttention forward kernel write to HBM for each query row, and why?
options: The full row of $P$, so the backward pass can reuse it
The log-sum-exp $L = m + \log l$, so the backward pass can recompute $P$ from $Q$ and $K$ without storing it
Nothing else; the backward pass recomputes $m$ and $l$ from scratch with a separate reduction
The running max $m$ only, since $l$ can be derived from $O$
explain: Algorithm 1 in the FlashAttention-3 paper ends by writing $O_i$ and $L_i = m_i + \log(\ell_i)$. One number per row is enough to recompute $P = \exp(S - L)$ block by block in the backward pass, which is how FlashAttention avoids storing the $N \times N$ matrix.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-4 forward: when the exponential is the bottleneck
question: A Blackwell softmax thread owns one full 128-element row of the FP32 score tile, plus that row of $P$ in BF16. If the row of the FP32 output accumulator ($d = 128$) also had to stay in its registers, as Hopper accumulators do, how many registers would that take?
options: 192, which fits comfortably
64, because BF16 values pack two per register
128, because S and O can share registers
320, more than the 255 a thread can have
explain: 128 for the FP32 scores, 64 for $P$ packed two per register, and 128 for the FP32 output row: 320. A thread can use at most 255, so this layout only works because tensor memory holds $S$ and $O$ and the thread borrows one row at a time. Sharing registers between $S$ and $O$ is impossible while both are live.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Why LLM serving needs its own attention engine
question: Which of these does FlashInfer treat as run-time input to its scheduler rather than as a compile-time kernel parameter?
options: The head dimension
Whether logits are soft-capped
The KV length of each request in this step
The data type of the KV cache
explain: Head dimension, the variant (such as soft-capping) and dtypes are fixed when the kernel is JIT compiled. Per-request lengths change every step, so they go to the plan function, which produces a fresh work assignment without recompiling.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Tile sizes, GQA head fusion and JIT attention variants
question: You want attention with RoPE applied inside the kernel (instead of a separate RoPE pass that writes rotated Q and K to HBM). Which variant hooks do you implement?
options: LogitsMask
OutputTransform
QueryTransform and KeyTransform
ValueTransform only
explain: RoPE rotates query and key vectors before their dot product, which is exactly what the query and key transform functors are for. The paper uses them for fused RoPE in StreamingLLM. A mask or output hook acts too late, and values are not rotated.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Relation to diffusion, and rectified flow in Stable Diffusion 3
question: Why does SD3 sample training timesteps from a logit-normal instead of uniformly?
options: The velocity regression is easiest near t = 0 and t = 1, so spending more training samples on intermediate t gives a better model
Uniform sampling makes the ODE solver unstable at test time
Logit-normal sampling removes the need for classifier-free guidance
It makes the paths straight without reflow
explain: Esser et al. argue that near the ends the target is easy to predict (close to pure data or pure noise), and confirm experimentally that rf/lognorm(0.00, 1.00) beats uniform rectified flow. It reweights the loss over time; it does not change the paths or the sampler.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Model checking a consensus core: votes, quorums and restarts
question: Which configuration makes TLC report a OneValue violation even with AllowRestart = FALSE?
options: 3 acceptors, quorum size 2
5 acceptors, quorum size 3
5 acceptors, quorum size 4
4 acceptors, quorum size 2
explain: Two quorums can be disjoint when 2 x QSize <= number of acceptors. With 4 acceptors and size 2, {a1, a2} and {a3, a4} share no one, so each can choose a different value. TLC's trace is 4 votes long.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Verus: proving Rust functions with requires, ensures and invariants
question: Which statement about Verus ghost code is true?
options: Spec functions can use u32 overflow semantics to match the code
Proof functions run at startup to check the lemmas
Spec and proof code are erased before compilation, so they add no run-time cost
Exec code may call spec functions to compute values at run time
explain: Ghost code exists only for verification. Spec functions use mathematical int and nat, proof functions are checked statically, and exec code cannot call either to compute run-time values.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Scaling factors: sliding a tensor into FP8's window
question: With delayed scaling, the scale for step t comes from amaxes recorded up to step t-1. A layer's activations suddenly grow 4x at step t. What happens at step t?
options: Training stops with a NaN because E4M3 has no infinity
The largest values exceed 448 after scaling and saturate to 448, so they are clipped for that step
TE detects the overflow and skips the optimizer step
Nothing: the scale is recomputed from step t before casting
explain: Delayed scaling reacts one step late. At step t the old scale pushes the large values past 448 and they saturate (clip). The new amax enters the history, so step t+1 uses a smaller scale. Current scaling avoids this lag at the cost of an extra pass over the tensor.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: When low precision fails: outliers, SwiGLU and debugging a run
question: Setting LLaMA2-7B's four massive activations to their mean values leaves the model working, while setting them to zero collapses it. What does that imply for quantization?
options: They are noise and can be clipped to the format maximum
They only matter at inference, not in training
They should be removed with weight decay
They are essential fixed biases: a quantizer must represent them, and must not let them flush their neighbours to zero
explain: Sun et al. conclude they work like constant bias terms. Clipping or zeroing them changes the model's function, and a shared scale sized for them can zero ordinary values: that is why per-block scaling, Smooth-SwiGLU style per-channel scales and higher-precision layers exist.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust and safety: what these teams defend
question: Why does OWASP say these automated threats rarely appear in Top Ten style vulnerability lists?
options: They misuse valid functionality rather than exploit an unmitigated vulnerability
They only affect small sites
They are illegal, so they are not security issues
They are always denial of service attacks
explain: OWASP's project notes that the events usually relate to misuse of inherent valid functionality. Excess traffic is sometimes mistaken for denial of service, but the DoS is a side effect, not the goal.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Network and device signals: IPs, proxies and fingerprints
question: Two attributes are independent. One visitor's value of the first is shared by 1 in 4 visitors, and their value of the second by 1 in 16. How many bits of surprisal do the two carry together?
options: 4 bits
6 bits
20 bits
64 bits
explain: Surprisal is $-\log_2 p$: 2 bits for 1 in 4, 4 bits for 1 in 16. For independent attributes bits add, giving 6 bits, the same as 1 in 64 (4 x 16).

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Finding rings with graphs: shared devices, cards and addresses
question: Adding 'same /16 IP block' as a link type suddenly merges 2 million accounts into one component. What went wrong?
options: Union-find has a bug with large inputs
A very common, weak identifier was treated as a strong link, so chaining connected strangers
The attackers are using IPv6
The graph needs to be directed
explain: A /16 block holds 65,536 addresses and often a whole provider's customers. Weak identifiers must be weighted down or excluded, or every component grows until it means nothing.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Card testing, 3-D Secure and strong customer authentication
question: During card testing almost every attempt is declined. Why does the merchant still suffer?
options: Declines are free and harmless
A high decline rate makes issuers and networks treat the business as riskier, raising declines for real customers; fees and disputes from the few that succeed add up
Declines delete customer accounts
The card network bans the merchant on the first attack
explain: Stripe lists reputation with issuers, fees, disputes on successful tests, load and polluted metrics. The decline-rate damage can outlast the attack.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Fake reviews and content abuse
question: Which of these does the FTC's 2024 consumer review rule prohibit?
options: Showing only verified-purchase reviews
Responding publicly to negative reviews
Asking all customers for honest reviews
Buying positive reviews or paying for reviews conditioned on their sentiment
explain: The rule bans creating, buying or selling fake reviews and buying reviews conditioned on their sentiment, among other practices. Asking every customer for an honest review, or responding to reviews, is not prohibited.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: The write-ahead rule: flush the log first, pages later
question: The buffer manager wants to write a dirty page whose page LSN is 4,812. What must be true first?
options: The transaction that last changed the page has committed
The WAL has been flushed at least through LSN 4,812
A checkpoint has completed since the page was changed
The page's full image has been written to the data file twice
explain: Write-ahead means log before data. Pages with uncommitted changes may be written (recovery treats transactions without a commit record as aborted), but the log describing every change on the page must already be durable, or a crash could leave a change on disk that no log record explains.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: What vulnerability research is, and the rules you work under
question: Which statement best separates a bug from a vulnerability?
options: Vulnerabilities are always memory corruption; bugs are logic errors
Bugs crash, vulnerabilities never crash
A vulnerability is a bug that lets someone break a security property such as confidentiality or integrity
A bug becomes a vulnerability once it has a CVE number
explain: Security impact is the difference. Many vulnerabilities are logic flaws, many crash, and the CVE identifier is just a label assigned after the fact.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Writing good harnesses: fast, deterministic and structure-aware
question: Why did the FuzzedDataProvider harness find the bug quickly even with comparison tracing off?
options: FDP disables AddressSanitizer
FDP contains a list of known bugs
It writes the magic and the record framing itself, so every input is structurally valid and only values are fuzzed
It runs more inputs per second than a raw harness
explain: Structure-aware harnesses move the format's rigid parts into code. The fuzzer's bytes only choose types, lengths and contents, so no effort is wasted on inputs the parser rejects at the first check.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Measuring fuzzers honestly: coverage, crashes and statistics
question: All 57,142 'unique' crashing inputs in cxxfilt were fixed by 9 patches. What does that measure?
options: That cxxfilt had 57,142 bugs
The speed of AFL
How badly coverage-profile deduplication over-counts real bugs
That stack hashing is perfect
explain: Grouping by fixing patch gives ground truth: 9 conceptual bugs. The heuristic inflated the count by thousands of times.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Symbolic and concolic execution: solving for the input
question: What does a path condition contain?
options: The list of functions called on the path
The concrete input that reached the path
The conjunction of branch conditions that must hold for execution to follow that path
The coverage bitmap for the path
explain: Each branch adds its condition (or its negation). Any input satisfying all of them follows the path; the solver finds one such input.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Why exact matching fails and what an edit distance counts
question: You know $d(a,b)=1$ and $d(b,c)=2$ under Levenshtein distance. What does the triangle inequality tell you about $d(a,c)$?
options: It is exactly 3
It is at most 3, and at least 1
It is at least 3
Nothing, because edit distance is not a metric
explain: The triangle inequality gives the upper bound $d(a,c) \le 1+2 = 3$. Applied the other way, $d(b,c) \le d(b,a)+d(a,c)$, so $d(a,c) \ge 2-1 = 1$. These two bounds are exactly what a BK-tree uses in lesson 5 to skip whole subtrees.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Levenshtein automata, SymSpell and fuzzy queries in production
question: With Elasticsearch `fuzziness: AUTO` (default 3,6), how many edits are allowed for the terms `ox`, `cat` and `kitchen`?
options: 2, 2 and 2
1, 1 and 2
0, 1 and 2
0, 1 and 1
explain: AUTO:3,6 means lengths 0 to 2 must match exactly, 3 to 5 allow one edit, and more than 5 allow two. `ox` has 2 characters (0 edits), `cat` 3 (1 edit), `kitchen` 7 (2 edits).

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: The Astrometry.net quad code, computed step by step
question: Your star detector has 0.5 px centroid noise. Which statement about the quad code is right?
options: Noise has no effect because the code is invariant
Noise moves the code slightly, by an amount that shrinks as the quad gets larger in pixels
Noise flips the parity of the code
Noise makes the code depend on rotation
explain: Invariance covers similarity transforms, not independent per-star jitter. Jitter moves C and D relative to A and B; in the unit frame the effect is roughly the noise divided by |AB|, so larger quads give more stable codes. In the toy, 0.5 px noise on a 323 px quad moved the code by 0.0044.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Distance on a sphere, and why degree boxes break
question: A service filters sensors with a box of plus or minus 0.01 degrees in both latitude and longitude around a point at latitude 60 N. What area does that box cover on the ground?
options: About 2.2 km by 2.2 km, a square
About 2.2 km north to south but only about 1.1 km east to west
About 1.1 km by 1.1 km, a square
About 1.1 km north to south and 2.2 km east to west
explain: 0.02 degrees of latitude is 0.02 x 111.19 = 2.22 km anywhere. 0.02 degrees of longitude at 60 N is 0.02 x 55.6 = 1.11 km, because longitude degrees shrink with cos(60) = 0.5. A radius filter built this way silently drops matches to the east and west.
